events.ctx: Nanakshahi New Year (Pehla Chet) marks the beginning of the Sikh calendar year, introduced to synchronize historical Sikh events with the tropical solar calendar. Commencing on Chet 1 (March 14), it commemorates the era founded in honor of Guru Nanak Dev Ji (originating in 1469 CE). The day is celebrated globally with special Gurdwara gatherings, Asa Ki Vaar Kirtan, and recitations of the sacred Barah Maha composition from Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji.

Hola Mahalla (often called Hola Mohalla) is a Sikh festival celebrated the day after Holi. Instituted by Guru Gobind Singh Ji in 1701, it is a time for martial displays, mock battles, and military exercises. Sikhs gather at Anandpur Sahib to watch and participate in Nihang displays of sword fighting, archery, and horse riding.
Hola Mahalla (year-end listing in 557). This entry represents the Phagan 557 date for the year 557 only.
Shaheedi Diwas (Martyrdom Day) of Akali Baba Phula Singh Ji, the Jathedar of the Akal Takht. He was a brave Sikh warrior who led the Akali army and attained martyrdom in battle.

Commemorates the victory of Sardar Baghel Singh (1730-1802), a Sikh military commander who captured Delhi in 1783. He forced the Mughal Emperor Shah Alam II to sign a treaty granting permission to build Gurdwaras at Sikh historical sites in Delhi, including Bangla Sahib, Rakab Ganj, and Sis Ganj.
Gurgaddi Diwas (Enthronement) of Guru Har Rai Ji as the 7th Sikh Guru.
Gurgaddi Diwas (Enthronement) of Guru Amar Das Ji as the 3rd Sikh Guru.

title.roman: 🙏 Jyoti-Jyot of Guru Angad Dev Ji

events.ctx: Joti Jot (merging with the Divine Light) of Guru Angad Dev Ji (1504-1552), the second Sikh Guru. Before his passing at Khadur Sahib, he nominated Guru Amar Das Ji as his successor, continuing the lineage of Sikh Gurus.

Joti Jot (merging with the Divine Light) of Guru Hargobind Ji (1595-1644), the sixth Sikh Guru who introduced the concept of Miri-Piri (temporal and spiritual authority). He passed away at Kiratpur Sahib after nominating his grandson Guru Har Rai Ji as his successor.

Shaheedi Diwas (Martyrdom Day) of Shaheed Bhagat Singh (1907–1931), the visionary Sikh revolutionary born in Banga, Lyallpur (now Pakistan). A passionate patriot who founded the Naujawan Bharat Sabha, he resisted British colonial imperialism with indomitable courage. Following the Lahore Conspiracy Case, he alongside Rajguru and Sukhdev embraced the gallows with smiles on March 23, 1931 in Lahore Central Jail at the tender age of 23, inspiring millions across India to rise against colonial tyranny.

Shaheedi Diwas of Bhai Subeg Singh and his 18-year-old son Bhai Shahbaz Singh (1745). Bhai Subeg Singh was a learned diplomat and Kotwal of Lahore who negotiated the Khalsa's treaty with the Mughal government that conferred the title of Nawab on Kapur Singh in 1733. When persecution renewed under Governor Yahya Khan, both father and son refused to renounce the Sikh faith despite being strapped to rotating wheels with sharp blades (Charkhari). They embraced martyrdom joyfully while reciting Gurbani.
Prakash Purab (Birth Anniversary) of Sahibzada Jujhhar Singh Ji. Second son of Guru Gobind Singh Ji, martyred at the Battle of Chamkaur (1691-1705).
Gurgaddi Diwas (Enthronement) of Guru Tegh Bahadur Ji as the 9th Sikh Guru.

title.roman: 🙏 Jyoti-Jyot of Guru Har Krishan Ji

events.ctx: Joti Jot (merging with the Divine Light) of Guru Har Krishan Ji (1656-1664), the eighth Sikh Guru who became Guru at the age of 5. Known as the 'Bal Guru' (Child Guru), he served the sick during a smallpox epidemic in Delhi and contracted the disease himself. Before passing, he indicated his successor by saying 'Baba Bakale'.
Guru Tegh Bahadur Ji (1621-1675) was the ninth Sikh Guru who sacrificed his life to protect the freedom of religion for all people.
Guru Arjan Dev Ji (1563-1606) was the fifth Sikh Guru who compiled the Guru Granth Sahib and built the Harmandir Sahib (Golden Temple) in Amritsar.

World Sikh Dastar Day (International Turban Day) is observed annually on April 13, coinciding with Vaisakhi. It celebrates the Dastar (turban), the sacred crown of royalty, equality, self-respect, and spiritual sovereignty bestowed upon Sikhs by Sri Guru Gobind Singh Ji. The day aims to raise global awareness about the religious significance and sanctity of the Sikh turban.

Khalsa Sajna Divas (Baisakhi) commemorates the founding of the Khalsa Panth by Guru Gobind Singh Ji on March 30, 1699 at Anandpur Sahib. On this day, the Guru initiated the Panj Pyare (Five Beloved Ones) and established the order of the Khalsa, transforming Sikhs into Saint-Soldiers committed to righteousness.

Guru Nanak Dev Ji (1469-1539) was the founder of Sikhism and the first of the ten Sikh Gurus. His teachings emphasized the importance of one God, equality of all human beings, and the necessity of leading a truthful life.
Guru Angad Dev Ji (1504-1552) was the second Sikh Guru who formalized the Gurmukhi script and made it easier for people to learn to read the Guru Granth Sahib.

Prakash Purab (Birth Anniversary) of Bhagat Dhanna Ji, a 15th-century saint and humble farmer born in Dhuan Kalan village near Tonk, Rajasthan. Known for his childlike innocence, unshakable faith, and pure devotion, he realized the Divine in everyday life. Three of his sacred hymns are enshrined in Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji across Rag Asa and Rag Gujri, reminding seekers that God is attained through simple, heartfelt love without ritualistic pretension.

Prakash Purab (Birth Anniversary) of Sheikh Fariduddin Ganjshakar (Baba Farid Ji, 1173–1266), the renowned Sufi saint and father of Punjabi poetry. Enshrined in Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji are 4 Shabads and 112 profound Saloks of Baba Farid Ji (alongside 18 Saloks of the Sikh Gurus commenting in divine dialogue). His hymns emphasize sweet speech, humility, detachment from transient worldly illusions, forgiveness, and ceaseless remembrance of the Almighty.
Guru Amar Das Ji (1479-1574) was the third Sikh Guru who strengthened the tradition of free community kitchen (langar) and opposed the practice of purdah (veiling of women).

Jormela Muktsar commemorates the Battle of Muktsar (1705) where 40 Sikhs (Chaali Mukte) attained martyrdom after returning to fight alongside Guru Gobind Singh Ji. Led by Mai Bhago, they redeemed themselves and saved the Guru. The town was renamed Muktsar (Pool of Liberation) in their honor.

Prakash Purab (Birth Anniversary) of Sardar Jassa Singh Ramgarhia (1723-1803), a prominent Sikh leader and commander who founded the Ramgarhia Misl. He was known for his military skills and played a crucial role in Sikh confederacy politics during the 18th century.

Commemorates the conquest of Sirhind by Baba Banda Singh Bahadur in May 1710. After defeating the Mughal governor Wazir Khan, Banda Singh established the first Sikh rule in Punjab and razed Sirhind to avenge the martyrdom of the Chotte Sahibzade (younger sons of Guru Gobind Singh Ji).
Guru Hargobind Ji (1595-1644) was the sixth Sikh Guru who introduced the concept of Miri-Piri, symbolizing temporal and spiritual authority.

Chhota Ghallughara (Lesser Holocaust) occurred on May 1, 1748, when Mughal governor Yahiya Khan attacked a gathering of Sikhs at Kahnuwan. Despite being outnumbered, the Sikhs fought bravely. Though many were killed, the Khalsa emerged stronger, continuing their struggle against oppression.

Prakash Purab (Birth Anniversary) of Sardar Jassa Singh Ahluwalia (1718-1783), a prominent Sikh leader who led the Ahluwalia Misl. He was raised by Mata Sundri Ji and became known as 'Guru Ka Lal' (Beloved of the Guru). He played a key role in Sikh military and political affairs.
Gurgaddi Diwas (Enthronement) of Guru Hargobind Ji as the 6th Sikh Guru.

Saka Paonta Sahib (May 1964) commemorates the supreme sacrifice of Nihang Singhs who laid down their lives to protect and restore the sanctity and community control of Gurdwara Sri Paonta Sahib on the banks of the Yamuna River. Founded originally by Sri Guru Gobind Singh Ji where he composed sacred Gurbani (including Jaap Sahib and Chandi Di Vaar), the shrine's management was liberated following this tragedy.
Shaheedi Diwas (Martyrdom Day) of Guru Arjan Dev Ji.

Prakash Purab (Birth Anniversary) of Sant Jarnail Singh Ji Khalsa Bhindranwale (1947–1984), born in Rode village, Moga. Initiated into the Damdami Taksal by Sant Gurbachan Singh Ji Khalsa, he became its 14th Jathedar in August 1977. A charismatic orator and staunch preacher of Amrit Sanchar and Sikh identity, he led the Dharam Yudh Morcha for Punjab's political, economic, and water rights, and attained martyrdom defending Sri Akal Takht Sahib in June 1984.

Ghallughara June 1984 (Operation Blue Star) marks the military assault launched by the Indian Army against Sri Harmandir Sahib (Golden Temple) and Sri Akal Takht Sahib in Amritsar in the first week of June 1984. Occurring during the Gurpurb of Sri Guru Arjan Dev Ji, thousands of innocent pilgrims, children, and defenders, including Sant Jarnail Singh Bhindranwale, Bhai Amrik Singh, and General Shabeg Singh, attained martyrdom. The historic Akal Takht building was reduced to rubble and the Sikh Reference Library was burned. It remains one of the most agonizing chapters in modern Sikh history.

Shaheedi Diwas of Sant Jarnail Singh Ji Khalsa Bhindranwale and Bhai Amrik Singh (President of the All India Sikh Students Federation), who attained supreme martyrdom on June 6, 1984 defending the sovereignty of Sri Akal Takht Sahib against the military assault of Operation Blue Star.

Prakash Purab (Birth Anniversary) of Bhagat Kabir Ji (1398–1518), a revered mystic weaver from Varanasi whose profound Bani forms the largest contribution among Bhagats in Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji (227 Padas across 17 Ragas and 243 Saloks). Kabir Ji fearlessly rejected the hypocrisy of rituals, untouchability, caste superiority, and sectarian divides, preaching oneness of God (Ik Oankar) and remembrance of the Divine Naam as the only true path to spiritual liberation.

Jormela Ritha Sahib is an annual gathering at Gurdwara Sri Ritha Sahib, a historic Sikh shrine associated with visits by the Sikh Gurus. Devotees gather to pay respects and participate in religious ceremonies.

The Akal Takht (Throne of the Timeless One) was founded by Guru Hargobind Sahib Ji in 1606, directly across from the Harmandir Sahib. While the Harmandir Sahib represents spiritual guidance (Piri), the Akal Takht represents temporal authority (Miri). The Guru himself laid the foundation and built the platform with the help of Bhai Gurdas Ji and Baba Buddha Ji, without employing any outside labor. It serves as the highest seat of decision-making for the Sikh community, where matters of political and social importance are addressed.

Shaheedi Diwas (Martyrdom Day) of Baba Banda Singh Bahadur (1670-1716), the great Sikh warrior who established the first Sikh rule in Punjab after defeating the Mughals. He was captured and executed in Delhi after refusing to convert to Islam, along with his 4-year-old son.

Antim Sanskar (Cremation Day) of Maharaja Ranjit Singh (1780-1839), the 'Lion of Punjab' who established a powerful Sikh Empire. His reign (1799-1839) was marked by religious tolerance, military excellence, and prosperity. He was cremated at the Gurdwara Maharaja Ranjit Singh Samadhi in Lahore.

Miri Piri Divas commemorates the occasion when Guru Hargobind Ji wore two swords - Miri (representing temporal authority) and Piri (representing spiritual authority). This concept, introduced after Guru Arjan Dev Ji's martyrdom, established the Sikh principle of the Saint-Soldier, balancing worldly and spiritual responsibilities.

Shaheedi Diwas (Martyrdom Day) of Bhai Mani Singh Ji, a great Sikh scholar and companion of Guru Gobind Singh Ji. He was executed in 1737 by the Mughal governor Zakariya Khan for refusing to pay a tribute for celebrating Diwali at Harmandir Sahib.

Shaheedi Diwas (Martyrdom Day) of Bhai Taru Singh Ji, a devout Sikh who attained martyrdom in 1745. He refused to convert to Islam and accepted death rather than cut his Kesh (uncut hair), a core article of the Sikh faith.
Prakash Purab (Birth Anniversary) of Bhai Taru Singh Ji, a devout Sikh martyr who gave his life in 1745 protecting his faith rather than cut his sacred Kesh (uncut hair).
Guru Har Krishan Ji (1656-1664) was the eighth Sikh Guru who became Guru at the age of 5 and is remembered for his selfless service during a smallpox epidemic.

Shaheedi Diwas (Martyrdom Day) of Shaheed Udham Singh (1899-1940), the Sikh revolutionary who assassinated Michael O'Dwyer in London to avenge the Jallianwala Bagh massacre of 1919. He was executed in London and is revered as a national hero.

The Guru Ka Bagh Morcha (1922) was a key event in the Gurdwara Reform Movement. Sikhs peacefully protested against Mahant Sundar Das, who had illegal control of Gurdwara Guru Ka Bagh. Despite brutal police beatings, Sikhs remained non-violent, eventually winning control of the Gurdwara and demonstrating the power of peaceful resistance.

Annual Jormela at Sri Baba Bakala Sahib, commemorating the historic revelation of the Ninth Sikh Guru, Sri Guru Tegh Bahadur Ji, in 1664. Following the passing of Guru Har Krishan Sahib Ji with the words 'Baba Bakale', twenty-two imposter Sodhis set up seats claiming the Guruship. The wealthy merchant Makhan Shah Lubana, whose ship was saved in a sea storm by the Guru, arrived and tested each claimant with two gold dinars, discovering the true Guru in his subterranean meditation room (Bhora Sahib) and proclaiming from the rooftop: 'Guru Ladho Re' (The True Guru is Found!).

India's Independence Day (August 15, 1947) commemorates the end of British colonial rule. Sikhs played a significant role in the freedom struggle, with many Sikh martyrs sacrificing their lives. However, the Partition that accompanied independence caused immense suffering to Sikhs and Punjab.

Partition Prayer Day (Vibhajan Ardaas Divas) commemorates the tragic suffering, massacre, and catastrophic displacement endured by the Sikh community during the Partition of Punjab in August 1947. Millions of Sikhs were forced to abandon their ancestral lands, homes, and sacred historical shrines—including Gurdwara Janam Asthan Nankana Sahib, Sri Panja Sahib, and Gurdwara Dehra Sahib—in what became Pakistan, with hundreds of thousands martyred during the mass migration.

Shaheedi Diwas (Martyrdom Day) of Sant Harchand Singh Longowal (1932–1985), prominent Sikh religious and political leader who served as President of the Shiromani Akali Dal and Dictator of the Dharam Yudh Morcha. Seeking a peaceful resolution to Punjab's political turmoil, he signed the historic Punjab Accord (Rajiv-Longowal Accord) in July 1985 and was assassinated shortly after while praying at Gurdwara Sherpur.

Sampooranta Divas commemorates the completion of Guru Granth Sahib Ji. The final version was compiled by Guru Gobind Singh Ji at Damdama Sahib in 1706, adding the hymns of Guru Tegh Bahadur Ji to the Adi Granth compiled by Guru Arjan Dev Ji. It is the eternal Guru of Sikhs.
The Guru Granth Sahib is the central religious scripture of Sikhism, regarded by Sikhs as the final, sovereign and eternal Guru.
Gurgaddi Diwas (Enthronement) of Guru Arjan Dev Ji as the 5th Sikh Guru.

title.roman: 🙏 Jyoti-Jyot of Guru Ram Das Ji

events.ctx: Joti Jot (merging with the Divine Light) of Guru Ram Das Ji (1534-1581), the fourth Sikh Guru who founded the city of Amritsar. He passed away at Goindwal Sahib after serving as Guru for seven years, nominating his youngest son Guru Arjan Dev Ji as his successor.

title.roman: 🙏 Jyoti-Jyot of Guru Amar Das Ji

events.ctx: Joti Jot (merging with the Divine Light) of Guru Amar Das Ji (1479-1574), the third Sikh Guru who established Goindwal Sahib and strengthened the institution of Langar. He passed away at Goindwal Sahib after serving as Guru for 22 years, nominating his son-in-law Guru Ram Das Ji as his successor.

Annual Jormela at Gurdwara Kandh Sahib in Batala, Gurdaspur. Commemorates the holy marriage of Guru Nanak Dev Ji to Mata Sulakhni Ji in 1487 CE. The Gurdwara preserves the historic mud wall ('Kandh') beneath which Guru Nanak sat while an elderly woman warned him that the cracked wall would collapse upon him. Guru Nanak famously replied: 'Bhole Maai, eh Kandh sadiyan tak kayam rahegi' (O innocent mother, this wall shall stand for ages).

Commemorates the wedding of Guru Nanak Dev Ji to Mata Sulakhni Ji at Batala. The Guru's marriage established important Sikh traditions. Gurdwara Kandh Sahib in Batala marks the site where the wedding ceremony took place.
Gurgaddi Diwas (Enthronement) of Guru Ram Das Ji as the 4th Sikh Guru.

Annual religious gathering at Gurdwara Tap Asthan Baba Budha Ji in Ramdas, Amritsar. Venerable Baba Budha Ji spent his final years here in deep prayer and meditation along the banks of the Ravi River. Guru Hargobind Sahib Ji traveled personally to Ramdas to serve Baba Budha Ji in his last hours and performed his cremation ceremonies with his own hands in 1631 CE.
Gurgaddi Diwas (Enthronement) of Guru Angad Dev Ji as the 2nd Sikh Guru.

Foundation Day of the Singh Sabha Movement, launched on October 1, 1873 at Manji Sahib, Amritsar, under the leadership of Sardar Thakur Singh Sandhawalia, Baba Khem Singh Bedi, and Kanwar Bikrama Singh of Kapurthala. Born in response to Christian proselytization and Hindu assimilationist pressures, the movement spearheaded a magnificent renaissance in Sikh literature, historical scholarship, Punjabi education, and pristine Gurmat identity, culminating in the establishment of Khalsa College Amritsar.

Joti Jot (merging with the Divine Light) of Guru Nanak Dev Ji (1469-1539), the founder of Sikhism and the first Guru. Before his passing at Kartarpur, he appointed Bhai Lehna (Guru Angad Dev Ji) as his successor, establishing the tradition of Guruship. His teachings of One God, equality, and truthful living continue to guide millions.

Annual religious gathering at Gurdwara Bir Baba Budha Ji in Thatha (Jhabal, Amritsar). It marks the sacred spot where Mata Ganga Ji, consort of Sri Guru Arjan Dev Ji, walked on foot with simple Missi Roti, Lassi, and crushed onion to seek the blessings of venerable Baba Budha Ji, who blessed her that she would give birth to a warrior Guru who would crush oppressors like an onion, foreshadowing the advent of Sri Guru Hargobind Sahib Ji.

Shaheedi Diwas of Bhai Harjinder Singh (Jinda) and Bhai Sukhdev Singh (Sukha), members of the Khalistan Commando Force who were hanged on October 9, 1992 in Yerwada Central Jail, Pune, for the assassination of General A.S. Vaidya, the Chief of Army Staff who commanded Operation Blue Star in June 1984.

Darbar Khalsa Dussehra represents the distinct Sikh tradition of celebrating the festival through martial vigilance, Shastar Puja (veneration of weapons as emblems of divine justice), and military exercises. Instituted during the era of the Sixth Guru Sri Guru Hargobind Sahib and fortified by Sri Guru Gobind Singh Ji, Sikhs assemble at Takht Sri Hazur Sahib, Akal Takht, and Nihang Dal centres to recite Shastar Naam Mala and reaffirm their duty as Saint-Soldiers protecting the oppressed.
Gurgaddi Diwas (Enthronement) of Guru Har Krishan Ji as the 8th Sikh Guru.

title.roman: 🙏 Jyoti-Jyot of Guru Har Rai Ji

events.ctx: Joti Jot (merging with the Divine Light) of Guru Har Rai Ji (1630-1661), the seventh Sikh Guru known for his compassion and healing abilities. He passed away at Kiratpur Sahib, nominating his younger son Guru Har Krishan Ji as his successor at the age of five.
Guru Ram Das Ji (1534-1581) was the fourth Sikh Guru who founded the city of Amritsar, which became the spiritual center of Sikhism.
Gurgaddi Diwas (Enthronement) of Guru Granth Sahib Ji as the N/A Sikh Guru.

title.roman: 🙏 Jyoti-Jyot of Guru Gobind Singh Ji

events.ctx: Joti Jot (merging with the Divine Light) of Guru Gobind Singh Ji (1666-1708), the tenth and final human Sikh Guru who established the Khalsa. Before his passing at Nanded (Hazur Sahib), he declared Guru Granth Sahib Ji as the eternal Guru of the Sikhs.

Saka Panja Sahib (1922) commemorates the sacrifice of Sikhs at Hasan Abdal (Panja Sahib). When a train carrying arrested Akali leaders passed by, Sikhs lay on the tracks to stop it and provide food and water. The train stopped, but many Sikhs were killed or injured. Their sacrifice remains a symbol of devotion to the Sangat.

Shaheedi Diwas of Bhai Beant Singh, who on October 31, 1984, assassinated Prime Minister Indira Gandhi following the catastrophic military invasion and desecration of Sri Harmandir Sahib and Sri Akal Takht Sahib during Operation Blue Star. He was shot and martyred immediately thereafter by Indo-Tibetan Border Police personnel in New Delhi.

Punjabi Suba Divas marks the creation of modern Punjab on November 1, 1966. Achieved through a 19-year non-violent mass movement led by the Shiromani Akali Dal under leaders including Master Tara Singh and Sant Fateh Singh, hundreds of thousands of Sikhs courted arrest demanding a Punjabi-speaking state with Gurmukhi as its official language. The struggle successfully led to the reorganization of East Punjab.
Prakash Purab (Birth Anniversary) of Mata Sahib Kaur Ji, the spiritual mother of the Khalsa.

Prakash Purab (Birth Anniversary) of Bhagat Namdev Ji (1270–1350), an eminent saint-poet from Maharashtra whose 61 sacred hymns are enshrined across 18 Ragas in Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji. Born into a calico-printer family, Namdev Ji's hymns celebrate intimate, ecstatic devotion to the Almighty, narrating how the Divine turned the temple of Dehra for him when Brahmins turned him away because of his low caste, asserting that the Lord belongs equally to all.

Bandi Chhor Divas (Day of Liberation) celebrates Guru Hargobind Ji's release from Gwalior Fort in 1619 along with 52 Hindu Rajas. The Guru refused to leave unless all 52 princes were also freed. Using a clever arrangement with 52 tails on his coat, all were liberated. This day coincides with Diwali and symbolizes the triumph of freedom over oppression.

Prakash Purab (Birth Anniversary) of Sant Kartar Singh Ji Khalsa Bhindranwale (1932–1977), the 13th Jathedar of the Damdami Taksal. A fearless preacher of Gurmat and ascetic scholar, he organized 37 massive Nagar Kirtans across Punjab during the Indira Gandhi Emergency to defy state repression and fearlessly awaken the Sikh youth to the ideals of the Khalsa.

Prakash Purab (Birth Anniversary) of Baba Budha Ji (1506–1631), born in Kathu Nangal, Amritsar. One of the most venerated figures in Sikh history, he was blessed as a young boy by Guru Nanak Dev Ji. Baba Budha Ji had the supreme honor of serving the first six Sikh Gurus and performing the ceremonial Gurgaddi tilak (coronation) for five Gurus (from Guru Angad Dev Ji to Guru Hargobind Sahib Ji). He was appointed the first Granthi of Sri Harmandir Sahib upon the first Parkash of the Adi Granth in 1604.

Antim Sanskar (Cremation Day) of Sardar Jassa Singh Ahluwalia (1718-1783), the leader of the Ahluwalia Misl who played a crucial role in Sikh military campaigns, including the capture of Lahore from Ahmad Shah Abdali's forces in 1761.

Shaheedi Diwas (Martyrdom Day) of Baba Deep Singh Ji (1682–1757), revered Sikh scholar, copyist of Sri Guru Granth Sahib, and the first Jathedar of Damdami Taksal and Shaheedan Misl. In November 1757, learning that Afghan commander Jahan Khan had desecrated Sri Harmandir Sahib and filled the sacred Sarovar, 75-year-old Baba Deep Singh Ji led a band of Khalsa warriors to liberate the holy shrine. In the fierce Battle of Amritsar, even after receiving a mortal neck wound, he fought onward wielding his heavy Khanda until reaching the Parikrama of Sri Harmandir Sahib, fulfilling his solemn vow.

Foundation Day of the Shiromani Gurdwara Parbandhak Committee (SGPC), inaugurated on November 15, 1920 at Sri Akal Takht Sahib, Amritsar. Formed during the historic Gurdwara Reform Movement (Akali Tehreek) to free historical Gurdwaras from corrupt hereditary Mahants and British interference, the 175-member committee was tasked with managing shrines under strict Gurmat principles, later statutorily enacted via the Sikh Gurdwaras Act of 1925.

Shaheedi Diwas (Martyrdom Day) of Shaheed Kartar Singh Sarabha (1896–1915), born in Sarabha village, Ludhiana. One of the most electrifying young revolutionaries of the Ghadar Party, he managed the revolutionary newspaper 'The Ghadar' in San Francisco before returning to Punjab to orchestrate an armed revolt against the British Raj among Indian soldiers. Betrayed by an informant, he was arrested and hanged in Lahore Central Jail on November 16, 1915 at only 19 years of age, becoming the legendary role model for Bhagat Singh.

Antim Sanskar (Cremation Day) of Bhai Mardana Ji (1459-1539), the lifelong companion of Guru Nanak Dev Ji. A Muslim by birth, he accompanied the Guru on all four Udasis (journeys) and played the Rabab while the Guru sang divine hymns. He was one of the first Sikhs and a model of devotion.
Prakash Purab (Birth Anniversary) of Sahibzada Zorawar Singh Ji. Third son of Guru Gobind Singh Ji, martyred at Sirhind (1696-1705).

Shaheedi Diwas (Martyrdom Day) of Nihang Baba Gurbaksh Singh Ji (1688–1764). During the seventh Afghan invasion in December 1764, Ahmad Shah Abdali marched upon Amritsar with 30,000 troops. Baba Gurbaksh Singh, along with a committed band of only 30 Nihang Singhs, stood guard outside Sri Darbar Sahib. Choosing martyrdom over surrender, they charged the Afghan vanguard near the Akal Takht, battling to their last breath to protect the dignity and sanctity of Sri Harmandir Sahib.
Gurgaddi Diwas (Enthronement) of Guru Gobind Singh Ji as the 10th Sikh Guru.

Shaheedi Diwas (Martyrdom Day) of Bhai Mati Das, Bhai Sati Das, and Bhai Dayal Das, the three devoted Sikhs who were tortured to death alongside Guru Tegh Bahadur Ji in November 1675 for refusing to convert to Islam.
Shaheedi Diwas (Martyrdom Day) of Guru Tegh Bahadur Ji.
Prakash Purab (Birth Anniversary) of Sahibzada Fateh Singh Ji. Youngest son of Guru Gobind Singh Ji, martyred at Sirhind at age 6 (1699-1705).

Foundation Day of the Shiromani Akali Dal, established on December 14, 1920 at Sri Akal Takht Sahib, Amritsar, as the task force of the Panth during the Gurdwara Reform Movement. Dedicated to liberating historic Gurdwaras from corrupt Mahants through non-violent agitation, the Akali Dal unified regional Jathas under a single leadership (with S. Sarmukh Singh Jhabal as its first president) and went on to play a pivotal role in India's independence struggle.

Sis Ganj Sahib commemorates the site where Guru Tegh Bahadur Ji's severed head was cremated by Bhai Jaita Ji after retrieving it from Delhi. Gurdwara Sis Ganj Sahib in Anandpur Sahib marks this sacred location, representing the Guru's supreme sacrifice for religious freedom.

Commemorates the evacuation of Anandpur Sahib by Guru Gobind Singh Ji and the Sikhs in December 1705, after a prolonged siege by Mughal and hill forces. Despite promises of safe passage, the Sikhs were attacked upon leaving, leading to the battles of Chamkaur and Muktsar.

Commemorates the separation of Guru Gobind Singh Ji's family at Sirsa during the evacuation of Anandpur Sahib in December 1705. Mata Gujri Ji and the younger Sahibzadas were separated from the Guru and later betrayed to the Mughal governor of Sirhind, leading to their martyrdom.

Shaheedi Diwas of Baba Jeevan Singh Ji (formerly Bhai Jaita Ji, 1649–1705). Following the public martyrdom of the Ninth Guru, Sri Guru Tegh Bahadur Ji, in Chandni Chowk, Delhi (1675), Bhai Jaita performed the perilous feat of retrieving the Guru's sacred head (Sis) and carrying it across hundreds of miles to Sri Anandpur Sahib. Guru Gobind Singh Ji embraced him, proclaiming 'Ranghreta Guru Ka Beta' (Ranghreta is the Son of the Guru). He was initiated into the Khalsa Panth as Baba Jeevan Singh, trained Khalsa warriors, commanded the rear guard during the evacuation of Anandpur at Sarsa river, and fell fighting valiantly at the Battle of Chamkaur.

The martyrdom of the Elder Sahibzadas, Baba Ajit Singh Ji and Baba Jujhar Singh Ji, occurred at the Battle of Chamkaur. Outnumbered 1 to 100,000, they fought with unprecedented valor. With their father Guru Gobind Singh Ji watching from the fortress, they entered the battlefield one after the other and attained martyrdom, proving that the Khalsa spirit is invincible even against overwhelming odds.

Shaheedi Diwas of Bhai Sangat Singh Ji, a devoted Sikh commander whose appearance closely resembled Guru Gobind Singh Ji. At the historic Battle of Chamkaur (December 1705), when the fortress was surrounded by hundreds of thousands of imperial troops, the Panj Pyare ordered Guru Gobind Singh Ji to depart so the Khalsa Panth could live on. Bhai Sangat Singh was placed in command, donning the Guru's Kalgi (plume) and royal Choga. Standing on the ramparts of Chamkaur Garhi, he kept the enemy forces engaged until his glorious martyrdom, ensuring the Guru's safe passage.

The martyrdom of the Chotte Sahibzade (Sahibzada Zorawar Singh Ji and Sahibzada Fateh Singh Ji) and their grandmother, Mata Gujri Ji, is a unique and incomparable event in world history. Sentenced to be bricked alive for refusing to renounce their faith, the young Sahibzadas (aged 9 and 6) stood steadfast. They were martyred at Sirhind, while Mata Gujri Ji breathed her last in the Thanda Burj (Cold Tower). Their sacrifice shook the foundations of the Mughal Empire.
Guru Gobind Singh Ji (1666-1708) was the tenth Sikh Guru who established the Khalsa and formalized the five Ks that Sikhs wear.

Shaheedi Diwas of Bhai Satwant Singh and Bhai Kehar Singh, who were hanged on January 6, 1989 in Tihar Jail, New Delhi, for their involvement in the October 31, 1984 assassination of Indira Gandhi following the military assault on Sri Darbar Sahib. Their mortal remains were cremated inside the jail premises without being handed over to their families.

Commemorates the laying of the foundation stone of Sri Harmandir Sahib (Golden Temple) in Amritsar on 1 Magh 1645 Bk (December 1588). In an extraordinary testament to universal brotherhood and the inclusive spirit of Sikhi, Sri Guru Arjan Dev Ji invited the venerated Sufi saint of Lahore, Hazrat Sai Mian Mir Ji, to lay the foundation brick. Designed with four entrances open to all directions, castes, and creeds, it stands as the timeless spiritual center of the Sikh faith.

Maghi Mela at Muktsar is an annual religious fair held on Magh 1 (January 14) commemorating the Battle of Muktsar (1705) and the martyrdom of the Chaali Mukte (40 Liberated Ones). Thousands of devotees gather to take a holy dip and pay respects at Gurdwara Sri Muktsar Sahib.

Chabiyan Da Morcha (Keys Agitation) of 1922 was a peaceful protest during the Gurdwara Reform Movement. Sikhs demanded the keys to the treasury of Harmandir Sahib from the British-appointed manager. Through non-violent resistance and negotiations, the keys were eventually returned to the Panth, marking a significant victory.

Prakash Purab (Birth Anniversary) of Baba Deep Singh Ji (January 26, 1682 – November 11, 1757), born in Pahuwind village, Amritsar. A foremost disciple of Guru Gobind Singh Ji, he mastered Gurmukhi, Persian, Arabic, and martial warfare. He assisted Bhai Mani Singh Ji in preparing handwritten saroops of Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji at Talwandi Sabo (Damdama Sahib) and founded the Taksal's exegetical and scholarly tradition.

The Vaddha Ghallughara (Great Massacre) took place in February 1762. The Afghan invader Ahmad Shah Abdali, determined to crush the rising power of the Sikhs, launched a surprise attack on a large gathering of Sikhs (Vahir) moving near Kup Rohira. The Sikhs, caught in an open plain with their families, formed a protective ring around the women, children, and elderly. In a single day of brutal fighting, an estimated 25,000 to 30,000 Sikhs achieved martyrdom. Despite this catastrophic loss, the Khalsa spirit remained unbroken, and they were able to liberate Punjab within a few years.

Commemorates the wedding of Guru Gobind Singh Ji. The Guru was married to Mata Jito Ji (also known as Mata Sundri), and Mata Sahib Kaur Ji who became the spiritual mother of the Khalsa. These marriages took place at Anandpur Sahib.

Basant Panchami in Sikh tradition marks the arrival of spring and is celebrated with profound spiritual fervor, notably at Gurdwara Chheharta Sahib near Amritsar. Guru Arjan Dev Ji constructed the historic six-wheeled well (Chheharta) here to alleviate water scarcity, around which the community gathered. Kirtan is traditionally recited in Raga Basant from Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji, symbolizing spiritual blossoming and renewal.
Prakash Purab (Birth Anniversary) of Sahibzada Ajit Singh Ji. The eldest son of Guru Gobind Singh Ji, martyred at the Battle of Chamkaur (1687-1705).
Guru Har Rai Ji (1630-1661) was the seventh Sikh Guru known for his compassion and service to humanity regardless of their religion.

Prakash Purab (Birth Anniversary) of Bhagat Ravidas Ji, a visionary 15th-century socio-religious poet-saint from Varanasi. His 41 divine hymns across 16 Ragas in Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji articulated the immortal concept of 'Begumpura' (the City without Sorrow)—an egalitarian society completely devoid of caste prejudice, exploitation, taxes, and tyranny. His life exemplified dignity of labor and spiritual supremacy through pure inner devotion.

Saka Nankana Sahib refers to the massacre that took place at Gurdwara Janam Asthan in February 1921. At the time, many Gurdwaras were controlled by corrupt Mahants. A group of peaceful Sikh reformers (Akalis), led by Bhai Lachhman Singh Dharowali, entered the Gurdwara to reclaim it. The Mahant, Narain Das, and his mercenaries attacked the peaceful group with guns and hatchets, killing over 130 Sikhs and burning their bodies. This sacrifice played a pivotal role in the Gurdwara Reform Movement, eventually leading to the formation of the SGPC and the liberation of historical Gurdwaras.

The Jaito da Morcha (1923-25) was a significant non-violent protest for religious freedom and the restoration of the deposed Maharaja of Nabha, Ripudaman Singh, a supporter of the Akali movement. Peaceful batches of Sikhs (Jathas) marched towards Jaito to hold an Akhand Path (continuous scripture reading). They were met with brutal force by British-led troops, resulting in many casualties. The movement eventually led to the passage of the Sikh Gurdwaras Act in 1925, bringing Gurdwaras under community control.

Marks the completion and first installation (Pehla Parkash) of the Adi Granth at Sri Harmandir Sahib in 1604 CE. Sri Guru Arjan Dev Ji compiled the sacred hymns of the first five Gurus, fifteen Bhagats, eleven Bhatts, and Gursikhs, sanctifying the shrine as the dwelling place of the Word of God. Revered Baba Budha Ji was appointed the first Granthi, carrying the sacred Scripture on his head with Guru Arjan Dev Ji waving the Chaur Sahib.
Sangrand marks the beginning of the Chet month in the Nanakshahi calendar. It is a time for fresh starts, spiritual reflection, and community gatherings at Gurdwaras.
Sangrand marks the beginning of the Vaisakh month in the Nanakshahi calendar. It is a time for fresh starts, spiritual reflection, and community gatherings at Gurdwaras.
Sangrand marks the beginning of the Jeth month in the Nanakshahi calendar. It is a time for fresh starts, spiritual reflection, and community gatherings at Gurdwaras.
Sangrand marks the beginning of the Harh month in the Nanakshahi calendar. It is a time for fresh starts, spiritual reflection, and community gatherings at Gurdwaras.
Sangrand marks the beginning of the Sawan month in the Nanakshahi calendar. It is a time for fresh starts, spiritual reflection, and community gatherings at Gurdwaras.
Sangrand marks the beginning of the Bhadon month in the Nanakshahi calendar. It is a time for fresh starts, spiritual reflection, and community gatherings at Gurdwaras.

Sangrand marks the first day of Assu (mid-September to mid-October), the seventh month in the Nanakshahi calendar. In Barah Maha (Rag Majh), Guru Arjan Dev Ji reminds seekers that true peace comes from love and remembrance of the Divine, as the heat of summer gives way to the gentle breeze of autumn.

Sangrand marks the first day of Katak (mid-October to mid-November), the eighth month in the Nanakshahi calendar. In Barah Maha, Guru Arjan Dev Ji teaches that all spiritual rewards are attained when the mind is attuned to the Lord's lotus feet, bringing illumination amidst the darkness.

Sangrand marks the first day of Maghar (mid-November to mid-December), the ninth month in the Nanakshahi calendar. In Barah Maha, the Guru reflects that those imbued with divine love sit gloriously in the presence of the Lord, unaffected by worldly sorrow.

Sangrand marks the first day of Poh (mid-December to mid-January), the tenth month in the Nanakshahi calendar. In Barah Maha, the Guru notes that the cold of winter cannot touch one embraced by the Lord's presence. In Sikh history, Poh is revered as the month of supreme sacrifices by the Sahibzadas and Mata Gujri Ji.
Sangrand marks the beginning of the Magh month in the Nanakshahi calendar. It is a time for fresh starts, spiritual reflection, and community gatherings at Gurdwaras.

Sangrand marks the first day of Phagan (mid-February to mid-March), the twelfth and final month of the Nanakshahi calendar. In Barah Maha, Guru Arjan Dev Ji describes Phagan as a season of blossoming joy and spiritual union for those who have realized the Almighty.
